Thank you, Madam Chair. This report is a follow up to December 6, 2022, SPC on Finance Meeting, where committee directed the administration to report back on the impact of applying property assessment changes,

retroactively for properties who are impacted but did not file appeals. As outlined in the report, the intent of the current legislation is to provide an equitable distribution of the tax burden and a stable tax base for Saskatchewan municipalities.

A stable and equitable tax base requires finality in the assessment role, rather than an assessment role that is constantly subject to change. The Court of Appeal has repeatedly held that an assessment is presumed correct until an error is proven on appeal.

The city currently goes above and beyond legislative requirements to communicate when the role is open. It's importance and property owners ability to appeal. This includes advertisements in the local paper, public service announcements online and through social media, information videos and a tax calculator, so property owners can see the potential tax impacts of their assessment changes during the appeal window.

In the event of an appeal, Section 178 of the City's Act outlines corrections to the assessment role can be made in the current year only. It does not allow for application of board, committee or court of appeal decisions retroactively.

The provincial legislation varies across Canada in relation to assessment. However, in our discussions with other municipalities and review of other legislations, there were no examples the administration could find where municipalities either applied assessment decisions retroactively

or applied decisions in the current year to properties that did not appeal. Theoretically, if the city were to apply 2022 appeal results to the 2021 assessment role, there would have been $153 million assessment impact, resulting in property tax returns of approximately $2.4 million.
This number would fluctuate significantly from year to year depending on the appeals that are being heard and the time it takes to reach a decision which can take several years.
